name: Pliny the Elder
credit: Statue of Pliny the Elder (19th century) on the facade of Como Cathedral, photograph by Wolfgang Sauber (2006) · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gaius Plinius Secundus was born in AD 23 at Novum Comum (modern Como) in northern Italy and trained for a public career at Rome. He served as a cavalry officer in Germany, pleaded in the courts, and under Vespasian held procuratorships in several provinces; he was a friend of the emperor and of his son Titus. He was also a tireless reader and note-taker, who is said to have been read to while he bathed and dined and to have written in his litter as he travelled.

His only surviving work is the Natural History in thirty-seven books, completed about AD 77 and dedicated to Titus: an encyclopaedia of the world from cosmology, geography, anthropology and zoology to botany, medicine, metals, painting, sculpture and gems, drawn from some two thousand volumes by about a hundred authors. In AD 79 he was commanding the fleet at Misenum when Vesuvius erupted; he sailed across the bay to rescue those on the shore and died there, as his nephew Pliny the Younger recounts. This site carries the Bostock and Riley translation of 1855, beginning with Books I-V: Pliny's dedication and table of contents, then the books on the world and the heavens, and on the geography of Europe, Africa and Asia.
